intro: Madrid rewards unhurried days: world-class paintings in the morning, long lunches, royal streets, and neighborhoods that stay lively after dark.

places.name: Museo del Prado
places.why_go: One of Europe’s great painting collections, with Velázquez, Goya, Bosch, Titian, and Rubens in a grand but navigable museum.
places.description: Give the Prado at least two focused hours rather than trying to conquer every gallery. Start with Las Meninas, Goya’s Black Paintings, and Bosch’s Garden of Earthly Delights, then use the museum map to follow the artists that interest you. The building sits at the heart of Madrid’s museum district, so it pairs naturally with a walk through Retiro afterward.
places.how_to_get_there: Walk from Atocha or take Metro Line 2 to Banco de España; the main entrance is on Calle de Ruiz de Alarcón near the Paseo del Prado.
places.cost: Paid entry; standard adult tickets are commonly around €15, but check the official site for current prices and free-entry hours.
places.booking_tip: Reserve a timed ticket online for weekends and peak season. Arrive early or use a late-afternoon slot for calmer galleries.

places.name: Royal Palace of Madrid
places.why_go: Lavish state rooms, a monumental staircase, and sweeping views over the old city make this a classic Madrid first stop.
places.description: Although Spain’s royal family does not live here, the palace remains the ceremonial centerpiece of the capital. Its rooms layer frescoes, tapestries, porcelain, and royal collections on an imperial scale; take time for the Throne Room and the Royal Armoury if it is included with your visit. The surrounding Sabatini Gardens and Almudena Cathedral make this more than a quick indoor stop.
places.how_to_get_there: Take Metro Lines 2 or 5 to Ópera, then walk about five minutes west through Plaza de Oriente.
places.cost: Timed admission is generally charged, often roughly €14–€16 for adults; concessions and closures vary, so confirm before going.
places.booking_tip: Book ahead online, especially for mornings. Check the calendar because official ceremonies can alter access with little notice.

places.name: El Retiro Park
places.why_go: Madrid’s beloved green escape offers rowboats, sculpture-lined paths, a glass palace, and a welcome pause between museums.
places.description: Retiro is best treated as a flexible wandering space, not a checklist. Enter near the Puerta de Alcalá or Prado side, see the Crystal Palace and its changing exhibitions, then follow the water toward the Monument to Alfonso XII. Weekend performers and families give it a local feel, while shaded paths make it especially useful on warm afternoons.
places.how_to_get_there: Metro Line 2 stops at Retiro, and Ibiza on Line 9 is useful for the eastern side; several entrances are a short walk from the Prado.
places.cost: Park entry is free. Rowboats and occasional exhibitions may have separate fees or schedules.
places.booking_tip: No booking is needed. Go early on hot days and check official notices after storms, when areas can close temporarily.

places.name: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía
places.why_go: See Picasso’s Guernica in context alongside major Spanish and international modern art.
places.description: The Reina Sofía gives twentieth-century Spanish art the space and political context it deserves. Guernica is the emotional center, but the surrounding rooms—works by Dalí, Miró, and contemporaries—are what make the visit coherent. The museum’s former-hospital architecture, terraces, and adjacent Atocha district are rewarding even if you only choose a few collections.
places.how_to_get_there: Take Metro Line 1 to Atocha or Estación del Arte, or walk about ten minutes south from the Prado.
places.cost: Standard entry is usually paid and often about €12; verify current pricing and any free evening periods on the museum website.
places.booking_tip: Prebook a timed ticket in busy periods. Visit Guernica early and follow gallery rules about photography.

places.name: Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum
places.why_go: A superb, approachable survey of Western art that fills the gaps between the Prado and Reina Sofía.
places.description: The Thyssen’s former private collection moves from medieval religious panels to Impressionism, Expressionism, and twentieth-century works with unusual breadth. It is an excellent choice if one museum feels too narrow: you can trace changing styles in a single visit rather than cross the city. Its manageable scale and central location make it ideal for a museum-triangle day.
places.how_to_get_there: Metro Line 2 to Banco de España, then walk two minutes along Paseo del Prado.
places.cost: Adult admission is typically around €13–€15, with temporary exhibitions priced separately; check current ticket terms.
places.booking_tip: Buy online for a specific entry window during weekends or special exhibitions. Allow extra time if you want the audio guide.

places.name: Mercado de San Miguel
places.why_go: A handsome iron-and-glass market for a concentrated taste of Spanish tapas near Plaza Mayor.
places.description: San Miguel is polished, busy, and more of a grazing hall than a neighborhood grocery market, which is precisely why it works for a first sampling of Iberian ham, seafood, croquettes, and vermouth. Prices are often higher than at local bars, so treat it as a curated snack stop rather than a bargain meal. Stand at a counter, order a few small things, and continue into the old town.
places.how_to_get_there: Walk from Sol, Plaza Mayor, or Ópera; Sol Metro station (Lines 1, 2, and 3) is about seven minutes away.
places.cost: Entry is free; individual tapas and drinks add up quickly, commonly €3–€8 or more each.
places.booking_tip: No reservation is normally needed. Avoid the lunch and evening rush if you want room to stand and choose calmly.

places.name: Plaza Mayor
places.why_go: Madrid’s grand arcaded square is a theatrical window into the Habsburg-era core of the city.
places.description: Plaza Mayor has hosted markets, celebrations, and public spectacles since the seventeenth century. Today it is best appreciated for its uniform red façades, archways, and the way side streets spill into the square; stop briefly, then explore the lanes around it rather than lingering over an overpriced terrace meal. The nearby San Ginés area is a useful next stop for churros or an evening walk.
places.how_to_get_there: Metro to Sol (Lines 1, 2, 3), Tirso de Molina (Line 1), or Ópera (Lines 2, 5), then walk five to ten minutes.
places.cost: Free to visit. Café terraces charge tourist-area prices, so read menus before sitting down.
places.booking_tip: No booking required. Come in the early morning for photos or after dinner when the arcades are attractively lit.

places.name: Temple of Debod
places.why_go: An ancient Egyptian temple unexpectedly overlooking Madrid, with one of the city’s most popular sunset viewpoints.
places.description: Gifted to Spain by Egypt and rebuilt in Parque del Oeste, the Temple of Debod makes a memorable contrast to Madrid’s royal and baroque architecture. The small interior has limited capacity and occasional access restrictions, but the exterior, reflecting pool, and views toward Casa de Campo are the main draw. Visit with patience: sunset is beautiful but crowded.
places.how_to_get_there: Take Metro Line 3 or 10 to Plaza de España, then walk northwest through the park for about ten minutes.
places.cost: The park and exterior are free; interior access, when open, is generally free but capacity is limited.
places.booking_tip: Check current opening information before making a special trip. For a quieter visit, go well before sunset on a weekday.

places.name: Gran Vía
places.why_go: Madrid’s cinematic main boulevard is the place for landmark façades, theaters, shopping, and city energy.
places.description: Gran Vía is less a single attraction than a dramatic urban promenade. Walk it from the Metropolis Building toward Plaza de España, looking up at the early-twentieth-century architecture and theater signs rather than rushing between chain stores. Nearby side streets lead to better bars and meals, while rooftop terraces offer strong skyline views if you are willing to pay for a drink.
places.how_to_get_there: Metro stops at Banco de España, Gran Vía, Callao, and Plaza de España along or beside the avenue.
places.cost: Free to walk; shopping, shows, and rooftops vary widely in price.
places.booking_tip: Reserve theater tickets and popular rooftops in advance. Walk at dusk for lights, but watch belongings in dense crowds.

places.name: Puerta del Sol
places.why_go: The symbolic center of Spain is a useful orientation point with Madrid’s famous bear-and-strawberry-tree statue.
places.description: Sol is constantly in motion: commuters, shoppers, street performers, and visitors meet beneath the clock tower where Spain’s New Year countdown is televised. Find the Kilometre Zero plaque, photograph the Oso y el Madroño, then use the square as a launch point for the old center. It is more compelling as a lived crossroads than as a place to linger for long.
places.how_to_get_there: Sol is served directly by Metro Lines 1, 2, and 3 and Cercanías commuter rail lines.
places.booking_tip: No booking required. Keep valuables secure in crowds and avoid the square at peak protest or holiday times if you dislike congestion.

places.name: Matadero Madrid
places.why_go: A former slaughterhouse reinvented as a creative campus, ideal for contemporary culture beyond the historic center.
places.description: Matadero’s brick industrial pavilions now host exhibitions, design events, cinema, performances, and public spaces beside the river. Programming changes frequently, which makes it worth checking before you go; even without a ticketed event, the architecture and Madrid Río setting reward a detour. It offers a useful counterpoint to the city’s canonical museums.
places.how_to_get_there: Take Metro Line 3 to Legazpi and walk a few minutes; buses and the Madrid Río cycle path also serve the area.
places.cost: Many exhibitions and outdoor areas are free, while screenings and performances may charge admission.
places.booking_tip: Check the current programme and reserve for popular concerts or cinema. Evening events can finish after the Metro’s busiest period.

places.name: Barrio de las Letras
places.why_go: Literary Madrid comes alive in pedestrian streets marked with quotations, tapas bars, and hidden courtyards.
places.description: The Literary Quarter was home to writers including Cervantes and Lope de Vega, and its street pavement still nods to that heritage. Wander from Plaza de Santa Ana down Calle de las Huertas, peeking into small galleries and traditional bars rather than following a rigid route. It is a particularly pleasant place for an unhurried lunch or an early evening drink before nearby theater.
places.how_to_get_there: Walk from Sol, Atocha, or the Prado; Antón Martín on Metro Line 1 is the closest convenient stop.
places.cost: Free to explore; food and drink range from inexpensive tapas to pricier terraces.
places.booking_tip: No booking is needed to wander. Reserve dinner on Friday and Saturday nights, especially around Plaza de Santa Ana.

places.name: Mercado de San Antón
places.why_go: A modern food market and rooftop in Chueca, handy for tasting, people-watching, and a casual evening.
places.description: San Antón mixes market counters, casual restaurants, and a roof terrace in the heart of Chueca. It is a more contemporary companion to San Miguel, with enough choice for groups who want different dishes. Browse the ground floor, then head upstairs for a meal or drink; quality and prices vary by stall, so a quick lap before ordering pays off.
places.how_to_get_there: Metro Line 5 to Chueca is closest; Gran Vía and Tribunal are also within a short walk.
places.cost: Entry is free; expect central-Madrid market prices, often €10–€25 for a casual meal plus drinks.
places.booking_tip: Walk-ins work for counter food, but book rooftop or sit-down tables for weekend evenings when available.

places.name: Santiago Bernabéu Stadium
places.why_go: A must for football fans, with Real Madrid history and a strikingly modern stadium setting.
places.description: The Bernabéu experience is designed around one of football’s most decorated clubs, combining trophy displays, interactive exhibits, and views into the stadium when operations permit. Routes and access can change around match days, construction, and team events, so approach it as a flexible attraction rather than a guaranteed full behind-the-scenes tour. The surrounding Chamartín area is easy to reach and less touristy than central Madrid.
places.how_to_get_there: Take Metro Line 10 to Santiago Bernabéu; Nuevos Ministerios offers additional Metro and Cercanías connections nearby.
places.cost: Tours are paid and commonly cost several dozen euros; match tickets are separate and can be much more expensive.
places.booking_tip: Buy official tour or match tickets well ahead. Recheck access rules the day before because event operations can change the route.

places.name: Lavapiés
places.why_go: A multicultural, creative neighborhood for independent cafés, global food, murals, and a less polished side of Madrid.
places.description: Lavapiés is best explored by following your curiosity through steep lanes, small squares, bookshops, and food from across the world. It has a strong local identity and a lively arts scene around Tabacalera and La Casa Encendida, but it is still residential—keep noise down late and support independent businesses. Come hungry, choose one cuisine or a tapas crawl, and leave room for a coffee in nearby Embajadores.
places.how_to_get_there: Lavapiés station on Metro Line 3 is central; Embajadores connects Metro Line 3 with Cercanías services.
places.cost: Free to explore; meals span budget-friendly international cafés to more polished restaurants.
places.booking_tip: No booking for a stroll. Reserve popular restaurants on weekends and use ordinary city awareness at night on quieter streets.
